claims.text: The Mg-5Al-3Zn-2Y-1Nd alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
Sintering the alloy at 920 °C under argon for 10 minutes will produce a dense, single-phase-like microstructure.
At 920 °C, an Mg-Al-Zn eutectic reaction produces a transient liquid phase.
Y and Nd suppress grain growth in the proposed alloy.
Y and Nd suppress Mg volatilization.
At 920 °C, atomic diffusion is sufficient to achieve more than 98% relative density.
Significant Mg vapor pressure and elemental segregation begin above 950 °C.
A heating rate of 10 °C/min minimizes thermal shock and volatilization.
The Mg-Al-Zn transient liquid phase facilitates rapid densification and homogenization.
Y and Nd form stable intermetallics that pin grain boundaries.
Y- and Nd-containing intermetallics inhibit Mg volatilization.
The transient liquid phase promotes rapid diffusion and pore elimination.
Y and Nd segregate to grain boundaries and form a protective layer.
The proposed grain-boundary layer reduces Mg loss and stabilizes the microstructure against phase-transformation instabilities.
The optimized material will have a grain size below 10 µm.
The optimized material will exhibit minimal elemental segregation.
The optimized material will have significantly improved oxidation and corrosion resistance relative to standard sintering between 800 and 1000 °C.
Standard sintering at 800 °C produces less than 90% relative density because diffusion is insufficient.
Sintering at 1000 °C causes more than 5% Mg loss.
Below 850 °C densification fails, whereas above 950 °C volatility and segregation dominate and cause microstructural instability.

contradictions.description: The mediator explicitly predicts stable Y- and Nd-containing intermetallic phases, while the outcome describes the product as single-phase-like without defining an allowable secondary-phase fraction.

The mechanism requires Y and Nd segregation to grain boundaries, whereas the predicted outcome calls for minimal segregation; no distinction is made between beneficial grain-boundary segregation and detrimental bulk-scale segregation.
